headline: CENTCOM's Hormuz numbers don't settle the oil risk
standfirst: The US military reports thousands of assisted ship transits and substantial crude support. That sounds reassuring, but it does not establish how much oil is moving through Hormuz today.
whatChanged: In a statement published on 25 October, CENTCOM said it had supported more than 3,000 commercial-vessel transits over six months and helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels since summer. Those figures are CENTCOM's cumulative claims, not independently measured daily flow.
whyItMatters: Tankers need safe passage, and insurers charge more when that looks uncertain. If ships can keep moving, some oil supply fears could ease. But six-month voyage totals and oil barrels measured from an unspecified summer start do not tell us whether export capacity is recovering now. No matching post-announcement Brent or equity-market reaction was established at this Pulse cutoff.
countercase: CENTCOM is a conflict participant reporting its own assistance. The voyage, cargo and safety measures may cover different periods and vessels. Reuters reported continuing attacks in October; independently observed AIS crossings, port loadings and insurance premiums would be needed to test the more optimistic reading.
watchNext: Compare dated UKMTO/JMIC vessel observations with port cargo data and insurer updates. Then check the first liquid Monday Brent, gold and US yield session before describing a price reaction.
